Joe Magnarelli

Trumpeter Joe Magnarelli is a native of Syracuse, NY and established himself in New York City in 1986. He has performed in the big bands of Lionel Hampton and Maria Schneider and in combos with Brother Jack McDuff and Ray Barretta. Joe has recorded as a leader on Criss Cross Records while finding time to teach at New Jersey City University.
Joe was interviewed on April 25, 2010 in Utica, NY, by Monk Rowe, director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and we are in Utica, in a coffee shop after a great concert with Joe Magnarelli. Welcome.
Thank you.
It’s interesting, we’re in Utica, and you think well like jazz in Utica in Upstate New York, but you sort of had an aha moment in Syracuse with Sal Amico you were talking about?

Yeah, well that’s why I got really inspired to make jazz my life and my career. It was the summer of 1983 I think it was, and Sal Amico and J.R. Montrose were working in Syracuse every Wednesday, I think it was every Wednesday and Thursday. And I would sit in and play as much as I could, and I was so turned on by the music. Also Joe Romano played there and Andy Krupsky from New York came up and played. There was a trumpet player from Pittsburgh also, Danny Conn. He passed away recently, but he was a great trumpet player from Pittsburgh. But yeah, great time.
When you went to see them, in your head were you thinking what the heck are those guys thinking about? How did they negotiate their way through these songs? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -1-

Yeah I thought that, sure. Yeah. I mean I was playing trumpet, not as a professional, but I’d been playing trumpet since I was twelve. And I played piano. You know standing on a bandstand with a rhythm section and improvising on songs, at that level, I had no idea like to learn how to do that. I had no idea.
Right. So if you asked Sal Amico about that, what did he tell you?

Well it’s funny I did sound him out about that. I did ask him. He never really told me. What he did was he accepted me for who I was, he didn’t [inaudible] me the situation. He understood my hunger for the music. And what he did do was he turned me on to the right records. And that was the greatest lesson really I ever had, the first four or five times I went to his house. He did write some things out for me to practice. He heard me play, you know I sat in in the club. So he knew where I was at. He gave me some things to practice and I practiced them. But he never really told me how he does it or how it’s done. And I think he probably thought that, knowing Sal, after I’d known him, of course he passed away, but I’d known him for like fifteen years, I think he probably thought he wasn’t worthy or he couldn’t really do that.
Isn’t there something to be said though for getting that inspiration and then finding out on your own?

Well yeah, and I think that he understood that aspect of it. And J.R. too. J.R. was very instrumental to me too, to my development too, and I would sit in with J.R. at the same time. And I would go to Sal’s house and then I would come back the next day and go to Utica College and play under J.R. J.R. was more of a mathematician. J.R. actually wrote down specific patterns for me to play. And he would tell me about my articulations, you know, like how to practice my articulations. And J.R. was more like a mechanical teacher, which was very good because to play jazz music on a high level, you have to have a lot of mechanics. You have to have things that you can go to, you know, things that are under your fingers or in your ears or in your muscles whatever you want to say. And having had those things built up, because there are times when you just have to use those things. And he gave me a lot of that stuff to practice.
The times that you use those things you’re talking about, your sort of finger patterns or things that you know will work, is that because your mind is not telling you to do something else?

Well there are times when you’re playing music — I mean I can just speak for myself — when I’m maybe not feeling as inspired. It might not be my fault. It could be totally my fault. It could be that I partied too hard that week and my brain is shut off. And that’s not really an excuse but there are times when you have to go into your bag of tricks and maybe say let me pull this out here and see where it takes me whether it’s some kind of a pentatonic thing that you’ve worked out, or maybe it’s a circle of fifths thing, or maybe © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-

it’s playing in half steps. These are things that you have worked out. Now I don’t go to a gig and plan to do these things. I never do that. But I do get in situations where — I am in situations where, yeah, I need to go there. And then I did a lot of big band stuff. You know I’ve played with many big bands, you know, the Glenn Miller Band and Toshiko Akiyoshi and Lionel Hampton, and a lot of times in those bands you only have 16 bars, 24 bars, and you can’t really be in a situation where you say well I’ll take my time and see what happens, no. You have to come out blasting. But again blasting, it’s got to be musical blasting. So you have to have those things ready to go, and J.R. was good for that. And that’s a very saxophone thing. Because you know saxophone players are generally the ones in big bands who play the most. And you know when they were on the road they’d play every night and they’d play the same tunes every night, because they had their devices that they used you know. And as the jazz trumpet evolved, the jazz trumpet players also started to develop these devices, in the sixties.

On your Web site I think it was a video lesson on a Web site and you said you have to have big ears and you have to be an ear player, so you’re trying to play things that you’re hearing. How do you get a student to hear those things?

Well you develop your ear. In the world we live in right now jazz is not a thing that you hear on any street corner obviously, you have to go find it. So I try to tell my students to do what I did and that’s transcribe, literally develop your ear. Having a good ear is something you’re born with as far as if you have any kind of musical talent, any kind of ear, you can develop it. You know some people don’t have to develop it because their hearing is so great that they can just sit around and pet their dog all day and listen to a record — I know people like this, literally — and they can listen to records and it’s there. You know that’s the kind of ears they have. They never transcribed anything and they have a whole history of jazz in their brain. Then there’s people like me who were born with a pretty good ear for music but I still transcribe every day. I transcribed on the way to the gig [inaudible]
I think you can get arrested for that. Transcribing while driving.

Well transcribing, what I mean by that, just to clarify, I just ear train. And I ear train by listening to Sonny Rollins and trying to hear what he did in the 60’s or Ornette Coleman. I try to diversify, you know, don’t just stay with one kind of music. Sometimes I’ll listen to Bach partitas or 18 bars of Mozart or something. Just try to develop your ear that way. That’s what I’m talking about.

Do you ever get students now that come in knowing more than you do about the theory of jazz, or stuff that they’ve learned. They may have a high school teacher who went to music college for jazz and they have imparted things to them that you’re not familiar with. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -3-
To be honest with you, no. Because, no.
Well that’s good.

Because anybody who would be that person probably wouldn’t be studying with someone like me. Because I’ve been around a long time and I’ve developed a lot of things, theory-wise. I mean I’m not sure I can play them all, but I’ve studied them all. I’ve studied scores, you know, classical scores and Thad Jones and Duke Ellington scores, and I’ve seen a lot of harmonic complexity, there’s nothing that really throws me, as far as talking theory. Now what I can actually play, that’s something I’m still working on. I mean I’ve had students come to my house that I felt were better players than me, just more natural trumpet players, that’s for sure. I mean I can name a couple. But yeah, as far as the theory, I didn’t go to school for music but I’ve really studied theory and just possibilities of harmonies and stuff.
Earlier you were talking about going to New York and you landed the Lionel Hampton gig and worked with Brother Jack McDuff I think, what kind of things did you learn from those guys, if anything?

A lot. Well with Lionel Hampton and Jack McDuff, both, I mean, just what they’ve done for me, I learned how to be a man. Because there was no room for weakness. You know, when you’re in a safe environment, maybe you’re weak sometimes and you get let off the hook. When you go on the road, you know being a young white kid going out on a bus with people that don’t look like you, it was an experience, it was a great experience. And in the beginning it wasn’t always friendly. But at the end it was a beautiful experience. And just about everybody that was on that band, and I wasn’t the only Italian or Irish guy on the band, but we were the minority on that band. And that was a good thing for us. That was a really good thing for us. Because I was forced to play my best at all times, or I could be ridiculed very easily. Now that doesn’t mean that — everybody lived in that role, not just me, it was everybody that was there. But I had never been in an environment where it was that rough around the edges. And that was the best thing for me. It was the greatest thing I could have — I don’t think I would have got that with Buddy Rich or Woody Herman, although I would have loved to play with both of those bands because of the greatness of those bands, I would have learned a lot musically. But there were things socially that I learned with Lionel Hampton that really were great for me.
That’s interesting, that sort of self-policing there by keeping the standard high.
Keeping the standard high, and no room for weakness basically. There was no sympathy happening. And I had just moved to New York. I was there less than a year when I got the gig.
Yeah. What was Lionel like personally? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

Well I never really hung out with him. He was 78 years old when I got the gig. But he was cool man. This was before he had his first stroke. He was still very strong. I mean he, I don’t know how to explain it but like when you stood next to him and you wanted to play the solo, but he was still playing the solo when you were playing the solo. He was still getting the house while you were playing the solo, okay? And that was the rule. Yeah he didn’t make it easy, man. Like you had to play over him. You had to fight for your certain sound, to get your stuff out there. Because again, it was really good, really good. It makes you strong. Because you said I’ve got to really be efficient on my instrument. I’ve got to learn how to play my instrument better, to get a stronger sound, so that it would carry. It has more of a sonority up there. And it reaches out over the sound that’s happening. Even though the sound that was happening was a good sound, but it was a strong sound. And my sound had to soar over that if I was going to take a solo. Plus he also forced me to play first trumpet which was something that was foreign to me. That was an experience that I failed at. So he got somebody else in about six months. But that six months he made me to play lead really helped my trumpet playing.
Were you there at the same time as Byron Stripling?
No, Byron was there before me. He was there for a short time then he went with Basie.
Does — you moved to New York in the late 80’s?
Okay. Have things gotten more difficult as far as your day-to-day, week-to-week landing gigs?
Landing gigs.
Yeah.

Well you know the way it is now the whole thing has changed. Now you have to go through yourself, you have to take care of your own publicity, and that’s really hard for me to do that. I’d much rather just go out and work, but I got to the point now where I really have to be a leader sometimes. And that’s a hard thing for me. I really just sit home and practice and work on music, and think about music, and then enjoy life too. So it’s a lot for me to handle. I’m doing the best I can. I’m staying busy and it’s okay so far. But yeah, it is a lot harder.
It’s like the whole other side of being a musician or an artist, like now there’s the business too.

Yeah, there’s the business and because you know it’s 2010 and the actual record business, which is CD’s or MP3’s it’s so weak. The percentage of sales is way down from even ten years ago. It might be down 80 percent. It’s almost a fold. And so that makes it very hard. You know I can put out a CD with some really great musicians and a kid out of college can make a CD with friends and get the same packaging and put it in © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

the stores and it looks just like mine. And not that I’m putting somebody like that down, I’m just saying that when I started recording it was a special thing. You worked for a company. And even though companies in some ways took more money than they should have from the musicians and discriminated sometimes and did some things, in some ways I think that environment was better than what is happening now.
At least there was a company.
Well at least there was a pecking order. You know there was a pecking order. You had to wait your turn. Now it’s like you want to make a CD?
Yeah. You don’t even have to leave your house.

You don’t have to leave your house. Sometimes the level, the level. It doesn’t matter what the level is, it’s about having a CD. And I’m looking for the right word. I guess it’s just cheapens everything. It cheapens the whole industry.

It makes, technology seems to me, in my generation, it seems to make things a little too easy or something. Well, time does go by. I was listening to you play today and I’m trying to get a handle on what you think about, if you’re playing a tune like let’s say “Countdown,” it’s pretty darn hard and the tempo is pretty bright. Are the chord changes going by in your head? And are you trying to choose notes from them?

Well in “Countdown” [inaudible] I had to play it once with a band. I’ve gone through “Countdown,” I’ve gone through “Satellite.” I like to play “Satellite.” I like to play “Giant Steps,” so I’m familiar with that, but “Countdown” is actually the hardest song I think. It’s more difficult. Because people like to play it like [scats]. I’m singing “Satellite,” but anyway “Countdown” the tempo is like [scats] and the changes move really quick. So yeah, I do think about the changes and I do actually have things worked out basically, I have devices worked out and so those moments when I may try to be creative and then the creativity leaves me because it’s so hard. I can go back to the devices. And to play a tune like “Countdown” you really have to have a lot of devices. Because you know I transcribed Coltrane’s second solo [inaudible] a month later, in fact it was called “Countdown” and he played all the same tunes again, and I transcribed that one. And Trane does the same thing. He has devices that he plays over and over again but he has so many of them and he’s so diverse, you know he has not an unlimited supply but he has a lot of devices because it doesn’t sound like he’s doing it. But if you transcribe that solo you can see the things he’s worked out, the way he gets through things. The same thing with “Satellite.” And “Giant Steps” is my favorite. I think that he plays so creatively on “Giant Steps.” There are some things that he repeats here and there but there are also times on “Giant Steps,” especially the second one, where he just seems like he found it right there on the tape. It’s a little disjointed in the rhythms, like the rhythm is © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-
a little stronger because he’s slipping and sliding around and it’s like wow, that’s really beautiful.
I guess that’s what transcription does for you. It really spotlights those moments where he’s not quite where he wants to be and then bam, he launches into it.

Yeah, to answer your question on a tune like “Countdown” I definitely play with the changes. That’s actually that’s a good way that’s the only way to practice for me. If you get a tempo in my head, you just listen to the changes go by in my head without a recording. So I’ll maybe get the tune in my head, playing it on the piano or listening to the record and then just sit in a chair and see the tune going by in my head. It’s good training. Because when you’re playing that’s what you have to do. So it’s good to see the tune just keep going by in your head, intently.
Let’s go back a little farther. Your Italian heritage — any music, was music strong in your family?

Well not jazz music but music was, yeah. Oh sure. My mom loved music, she was into Tom Jones and Andy Williams, and those are two of the great singers. You know now that I’m older I realize that. And my dad was always into show music, Broadway show music he listened to beautiful Broadway show scores and overtures.
Hip songs.
Hip songs. So I was very much into that kind of thing.
What about this church thing you did playing piano?

Central Baptist Church on East Brighton Avenue in Syracuse. Yeah. Well the story for that is I went down to New York to take a trumpet lesson with Carmine Caruso and I took the train back. And on the train back I met a preacher, his name was LeRoy Gainey. And he was from the Bronx, where I live now. And he was going to Syracuse. This wasn’t a trip to Syracuse, but he was about to move to Syracuse to take over this church. So we got to talking and the thing we had in common was basketball. So we started talking about it. You know it’s a six hour train ride from New York to Syracuse so we started talking about basketball, then we started talking about music, and he was very interested in what I was doing and all that. He was one of my best friends. Really he was great guy. And so he asked me if I wanted to be the piano player at the church when he was going to start. And I said I would love to. And the first week it was him and his wife, his two daughters, and three little old ladies who were from the previous church. And that was the congregation that day. When I left, about a year and a half later, we had about 400 people in the congregation. And the reason why I left, well I went to college, but the real reason why I left was because I wasn’t proficient enough on the piano for what they wanted. You know it became a real Gospel type congregation. And for a while I was hanging in there. I love Gospel music, I still love Gospel music and I love the way the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

Gospel piano style, Andy Crouch and Cleveland and all those guys, the piano players, I love their style. But I didn’t practice that stuff. I was more into studying the trumpet. And I was going to school and I was playing basketball. So he brought in another — her name was Minnie Pearl.
Minnie Pearl?

Minnie Pearl. And she was an established organ player in Syracuse. So she came in, and plus they used an organ. They couldn’t do a piano. But I will say one thing about working in that church. I didn’t go to the music school, I didn’t have the experience of playing in orchestras and all that stuff. But on Sunday morning at 11:00 when you have about a hundred people in the congregation and you’re playing the piano and they’re singing hymns, you can not screw up, and your sense of time and coordination really is at a high level. Because, like a couple of times it happened in the beginning where I could like screw up and the whole thing falls apart, and you just feel this energy coming at you, this negative energy, even though it’s church, it’s still there. And what an education that was for me. Just — it wasn’t about playing or chops or anything, it was just about knowing how to be in a band, and I was the band, I was the only band. And I just gained a significant education through this. It was something I’m really glad I did.
I know that accompanying can be a high pressure situation.

And then from that gig I got a bunch of like singers and would do these little cabaret gigs in Syracuse and I would play piano for them and it was really fun. And then again I was in a whole other culture. I mean I worked from the north side of Syracuse to the south side of Syracuse, you know I mean it was just like going out on a limb. And it was great. And I also, at the time, Reverend Gainey hooked it up so I was being paid by the city and they made the gym, which was downstairs, which was the cafeteria/gym, it was a rec center for kids in the neighborhood. So on Thursday nights and Wednesday nights I would supervise the basketball games and I would play too. So it was just great to be able to be in a whole nother world that I had no idea about, and really enjoy myself. It was really great.
That’s a great experience.
Yeah, it really is.
Are there issues these days, I guess they would go in a sort of political issues about gender or racial things or even generational things, that effect you’re getting gigs, getting recorded.

Yeah, no, it’s all there and it’s all palpable not enough for a breakthrough. You know there’s always room for a breakthrough. I mean if you’re being passed up because of race or gender or, the biggest thing really is generations, really. I mean sometimes people want to hear younger people. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -8-
People want to hear what?

Well I mean promoters and people who hire want young people, you know, kids. Sometimes they cost less. Yeah, I mean that’s actually the bottom line sometimes. But that stuff doesn’t is not to the point where it ruins it enough to want to get out. Because it’s not that strong. It’s not that strong. I mean musicians that I know, that are my peers, who maybe have a different color or are from a different culture, I never feel any vibe, ever. And if I do I’m at the point in my life now where I don’t even think it’s about race, it’s just about me. Insecurity about music. Or insecurity about themselves. I don’t even think quote unquote I’m white or something. I don’t even think it anymore. I just think if somebody [inaudible] maybe they’re insecure about their music or [inaudible] look like them too. And I don’t even think about it like that. But that stuff does go on outside of the music with promoters, with educators, that stuff does go on. But with people who can play I don’t feel it, I really don’t feel it. I feel like if you can play it doesn’t matter what you look like you’re going to be accepted. I’ve seen that in my life and I’ve felt it.
I’m glad to hear you say that.

Oh yeah. It happens. I mean [inaudible] and Tony Retis and Kenny Washington, you know, now, I’m not saying they’re not tough, they’re not like there’s a certain thing you have to pass through to be friends with them, but it’s musical. And it’s also personal too in a way, I mean they’re not going to want to be friends with you if you’re a bad guy, but you know, that being said, once you pass a certain musical threshold you’re cool. But I don’t think a guy like, let’s say Kenny Washington, the guys been on a lot of records and stuff. Well he’s a tough guy. But he’s tough because he’s a great musician. And he wants, if you’re going to hang with him and you’re going to talk about music, come in form, and be ready, be ready to like talk about some of these things. It’s also like that with Steve Kuhn or Joe Lovano, same thing, no different.
You’re not in the minor leagues now, when you’re with those guys.

Well yeah you’ve got to bring it. They bring it. Playing with Joe Lovano is no joke, because people want to [inaudible] okay just to give you an example and it’s not just to talk about Joe, but to give you an example of a guy people have many opinions. Because people sometimes they don’t understand the music. Joe Lovano is on a high level. He’s one of the best saxophone players I’ve ever heard. And he’s definitely one of the best players I’ve ever played with. And if you want to hang with someone like that you better bring some juice. And it’s funny because if you’re lucky you come with some juice, if you had a bad day the guy would be so understanding and so beautiful. And Kenny’s like that, and Mulgrew [Miller]’s like that. Beautiful people. I don’t know Mulgrew that well, I mean I’ve played with him a little bit. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-
As long as they don’t think that you’re just treading water or something, that you come to play.
If they think you’re shucking and jiving you’re gone. But if you come in like prepared, yeah, you’re cool.
What do you tell your students, five songs that you’d better know or don’t go to any jam sessions.
Five songs. Well one is the blues two is rhythm changes,
That’s a short list, obviously.

It’s a hard list. [inaudible] like “My Shining Hour,” “It Could Happen to You,” maybe “One Finger Snap,” you know, tunes like that. Because most of the young kids don’t know the repertoire of the standards or they’re really into the records more of like Herbie and Wayne Shorter, you know sixties, tunes like — what’s that tune — “Black Nile” and tunes like that.
Okay.
It seems like in New York anyway, because kids are into that now.
Did you do any of that seeking out jam sessions to sort of get your name out there?
Yeah. When I first came to New York. I don’t do it now but when I came to New York, sure.
How was it? Did you ever get embarrassed or have people make things hard for you on purpose?

I embarrassed myself a few times I think. You know the times I embarrassed myself was when I tried to play with singers and tried to play tunes indifferent keys and not really knowing the tunes. And I’ve done that a couple of times early in my career. But no I mean the only thing I can say is sometimes I was really overwhelmed, you know, just being on stage with really great trumpet players and realizing I had a lot of work to do. But that’s good in a way.

Right. If a parent comes to you and they have a son or daughter who is an aspiring musician and has got some talent and they say should I let my son or daughter try to go into jazz, has that ever happened to you?

Not really. What I would say is, honestly, what I would say is I would say if they wanted to get into jazz, if that’s what they want to do, and you’re worried about it, even though I’m really not a big proponent of jazz education in college, because I feel like if you really want to be a jazz musician the key to that is just getting the records that you love and learn them, and go out and play. The problem is going out and playing the part is so diminished these days that it’s not really, you know, I’m not sure that’s the best for a good kid. So what I would say would be this: have him go to school and get a music degree and get a masters. Because then they can have a teaching job and still play. And I © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -10-

had many friends of mine in college, they’re tenured, they’re in the school, they have a tenured job, they have a pension happening, but they still go out and do gigs, they do their thing, they write and they’re still growing as musicians. And I think if I was to give them advice, that would be the advice. Get a degree and get a masters. And then they’d be set. And you know what? Depending on how talented they are it doesn’t even have to be in music. It could be in anything. But I would say definitely get the papers. But if you want a degree, if you want a job in music you have to have a masters.
Did your parents tell you that, try to tell you that?

My parents were very, you know they backed me up in whatever I wanted to do. It was a different time. You know I actually went to school to play basketball. And they just wanted me to graduate. They wanted me to do well in school and graduate, which was really good advice. Because the times when I did slip a little bit, I think I was on probation one semester, you know they got down on me a little bit. So yeah, they definitely were strong for me to get an education. The music thing I think when I was younger they were like thrilled by that, but I think as I got older they were less thrilled because I think they saw the reality of the jazz situation. But I didn’t have [inaudible].
Right. You and I went to the same school. I went to Fredonia also.
Ah, yeah?
Before you.
Okay. I loved Fredonia.
They have a good jazz ensemble. I mean did you look at that from the outside and say I’d like to be in on that if I could?

Well to be totally honest, I went to OCC for a year and a half. And I was a music major for the first semester and then I dropped out and just became a liberal arts major. And I was playing basketball. And I didn’t have enough time to dedicate to music. Then I went to Berklee for a semester. And I loved Berklee. The only problem with Berklee was that every day at six o’clock I was at the Huntington Street YMCA playing basketball. Because really, I hadn’t faced yet, I was playing against all these football players who were great athletes [inaudible] they were just playing more Division I basketball. And I thought — I played one year on a basketball scholarship and I should try to play two more years before it’s over. So I went to Fredonia and I auditioned for the music department and I wasn’t accepted. So that’s what happened. And yes, I did look at it from the outside, although I have to say, Monk, that I may have played my senior year more than a lot of the music students. I was in the practice room all the time. I had gotten the Clifford Brown records and I just started. Nobody really told me what to do. I just started learning about three or four of those solos and I’d play them every night. And that was the thing that bridged me to Sal Amico, because I was hip enough that I knew three or © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-
four of those solos so I knew the phrasing and I knew what the sound was. So when I heard somebody do it live I was like wow. Okay.
And what’s this non-music-major doing in our practice rooms, right?

Yeah, well everybody knew me. They all remembered and knew me. Let me put it that way. But I didn’t have any chops so that was good, nobody felt threatened by me. In fact for a while I didn’t even have a trumpet I was on the flugelhorn. I was playing, a four valve Getzen instrument, which I still have.
If you could go in a time machine and go back to some musical moments in the history of jazz, do you have anything that you’d like to be?

Oh well I would have loved to see Charlie Parker. I would have loved to see Louis Armstrong in the 20’s, late 20’s, ’27, ’28. I would have loved to see Lester Young with the Basie Band in the 40’s, and Sweets Edison. I would have loved to hear Duke Ellington like in the 60’s. And I should say I would have loved to hear Louis Armstrong anytime [inaudible]. I would have loved to hear like Art Blakey’s bands in the 60’s. All that.
I hear some Art Blakey in your music. I mean I hear that kind of that unbridled energy in some of the tunes and stuff, remember that Blue Note —

I love that period. I love the 50’s, I love the 60’s too. I love the Freddie Hubbard band and the Lee Morgan band. But yeah, I [inaudible]. I love Bird too. Bird and Fats was probably my favorite band if I had to pick one, it would be with Bird with Fats, “One Night at Birdland” with Bud Powell and Tommy Potter and I guess Art Blakey is on the record. Roy Haynes sits in on the record. That’s one of my favorites of all time. I love Fats Navarro. He is one of my first influences. But after that period of Clifford, like at college, it was 1982, at the end of ’82 and ’83, that was where I missed out. I had got a Fats Navarro with the thing he did with Howard McGhee. And I copied all of his solos. You know, what I could play. Some of the stuff I couldn’t play. But the stuff that I could handle technically I played it every day with the tape.
In jazz improvising now, what constitutes a wrong note?

I think a wrong note is when you give up on that note. When you give up on it then it’s wrong but, because there’s no wrong notes, really, there’s no wrong notes. You can make any note valid on any chord. I mean think about it. If you have a G major chord and you play an A flat, depending on how you resolve that A flat, it could be a beautiful thing. Now if you go back to study classical music you’ll find things like that all over the place. And I think being sure of yourself and having faith in yourself to play something that doesn’t sound good and then play your way out of it. I mean I have done that. I played something I like and I’ll think to myself in that split second, wow, what was that, you know? And then I just play it again and develop that thing and bring it back into the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-
solo, that’s the key. But if you play something and you make a face or you musically give up on it, then it’s wrong.
Okay. It’s astounding to think what’s going through your head when that happens. Like the thought process.
It’s in a split second too. All the things that happen in that split second of your brain.
I like the little thing you said about just sitting and thinking about the chord changes, in time.
It’s good practice.
It’s very interesting.

It’s really good, because fast tempos, man, it’s all about being in sync. Like I know we talked about “Countdown” before, but let’s just say you want to learn how to play it fast. I used to play with a great drummer, Jimmy Loveless. You know he’s a New York guy, he played with Wes Montgomery and was on some of his records. But he was a real New York cat. And he used to play really fast. And I realized with him that you didn’t have to play every change. You just had to be in the vicinity of that sound. Every once in a while it was so fast [scats] and you didn’t have to play every chord change. You just had to be in the vicinity of it. You had to play your ideas and they had to be crisp and they had to be clear, but they didn’t have to be, you didn’t have to play every bar. You just had to be there. You know, okay there’s the bridge, now play the bridge. You know and then play something. That’s what he found. He didn’t play every chord change. He just marked them. But I’m talking really fast now. I’m not talking like uptempo. I’m talking like [inaudible] on the Sonny Rollins record. That kind of stuff. And sometimes it’s another way to practice. Because you can’t really practice that on a trumpet, it’s hard, to do that at home by yourself. So I used to just put on a record with a fast tempo and then get it really, get it all formed in my brain, you know, understand the form and everything, and then just sit there and think about it.
Here’s a question that sometimes is hard to answer, but do you have a best gig and a worst gig that stick in your mind?

Well the best gig is a hard one because I think the best gig was probably, just for like the prestige of it or the feeling, was when I played with Ray Baretto and we played the JC Jazz Festival at Carnegie Hall and we were playing my tunes in Carnegie Hall. That was, for a musician, jazz or otherwise, it doesn’t get much better than that, and being paid well. You know and the worst gigs, you know how that goes, there was some real bad ones but I don’t want to go there.

I know, most people don’t. Sometimes it’s not even the music it’s like getting home from the gig or this happened. Even coming here today you had some trouble, but that doesn’t make it your worst gig. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-

But you know the thing with me is that like I try to — whether I’m at Carnegie Hall and some band room in Vancouver, Connecticut giving a clinic to some middle school kids, I really try to go with the same attitude. Just play from your heart and try to play as best as you can and try to be a good trumpet player, and try to just play standard licks or whatever, you know, and that, so to me every gig is a challenge. It really is a challenge.

That’s a pretty good statement right there. I guess we could wrap up and get you to your next engagement. But I do think it’s neat that you said that one of your best things ever was hearing your own music. There’s something really special about that.

That was, if I had to pick one night in particular, that was, you know I’ve had many great experiences in music, you know, being a sideman with great singers or being on TV and stuff like that. You know stuff like that is exciting. But that hall like that, there is something about Carnegie Hall, there really is. I played in many great halls all over the world, and it’s really something special acoustically, you know, acoustically. It’s really incredible. Something happens there. There’s just a certain sound, the sound just gets carried like it’s beautiful.
What do you see yourself doing five years from now?

Well hopefully exactly what I’m doing now, with the exception of maybe writing more for hire. Hopefully, I just did a strings record, a record with strings, six different strings, and I didn’t do the string writing but the tunes are mine, the songs are mine, some of the songs are mine. Some are standards. And I did help with the string writing, let’s put it that way. But I didn’t do the strings. I made some adjustments here and there. And I want to start getting into more writing. That’s really my goal. But I also want to be a better trumpet player and trying to play better.
Where do your initial musical ideas come from? The piano? Or, when you write a tune.

Well it almost always came from the piano. But lately I find that it’s really good for me to just sit if you want to write a tune, and just sit down and play but what feels good on the trumpet. Something you have a feel for and then just try to expand on that until a song is born. And then the other thing that sometimes is good to do is write something at the piano and don’t worry about writing a song. Just write four bars or write six bars or eight bars, and put it in a notebook. And compile it. And then after a couple of months see what you wrote and you have all these little things and try to see where they all fit together, they come together to make a song. That’s [inaudible] what I do. And lately, the last couple of things I’ve written have been me sitting at home and just what feels good. You know, what feels good man. Like okay, write that down and expand, you know and formulate. I don’t know. I mean that’s not the answer. It’s just what I’m going through right now.
